newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Greenpeace to push into Asia and oppose oil growth.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace to push into Asia and oppose oil growth.

text.p: Greenpeace said on Friday it planned to expand into South East Asia and to increase pressure on the oil industry to cease further worldwide exploration.

Delivering the organisation's 1996 annual report, executive director Thilo Bode said Greenpeace's own development and successes were encouraging, but climate change and primary forest destruction continued largely unabated.
Greenpeace would continue to devote its attention to these two related problems, he said.
He also said Greenpeace recognised the need to expand its global presence with an office in South East Asia, in either Thailand or India.
Greenpeace opened an office in Hong Kong last year in what it describes as a first step towards planting the organisation in China.
"Greenpeace has to organise globally," Bode said.
The organisation hopes to match some of its successes in Latin America, such as in Argentina where its supporter base rose by 40,000 last year.
However, Bode acknowledged the "move East" could not be a simple expansion of current activities: it would necessitate new approaches suited to the cultural conditions.

"This presents us with a new challenge: how to export our successes to such regions, without making the mistake of dictating to people, of presuming we know best," Greenpeace said in its annual report.
Bode suggested confrontational tactics used in the West might not be suited to South East Asia and China.
"We have to show these people we can help them," he said.
However, campaign director John Hinck said low-key demonstrations in such countries, by virtue of their rarity, could attract much more attention than in the West.
"Confrontation has tended to be our best strategy," he said.
One area where Greenpeace expects some confrontation, as well as discussions, is in its strengthened attack on the fossil fuels industries.
"We'll have a particular focus on the oil companies... We call for an immediate halt to exploration of coal and oil and to replace fossil fuels with renewable energy," Hinck said.
He acknowledged Greenpeace's aims were ambitious.
"It's an enormous undertaking. (Fossil fuel companies) are among the most powerful the world has ever known," he said.

Greenpeace said it has already had discussions with senior management of oil giant Royal Dutch/Shell, but while Shell appeared to recognise the issue of global warming, Greenpeace said it had secured no commitment to downscale exploration activities.
"Shell's corporate plan continues to allow them to find every last barrel of oil in the world and to burn it," Hinck said.

Despite a worsening environmental picture in 1996, Greenpeace said it had achieved a number of advances with its campaigns and particularly welcomed the signing in September 1996 of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty by the five main nuclear powers.
"(It) marked the culmination of Greenpeace's longest running campaign," Greenpeace's annual report said.
Bode described Greenpeace's 1996 financial performance as "satisfactory" with grants and donations reaching 136.9 million dollars, slightly down from 1995's record 138.3 million dollars.
The apparent decline was largely the result of the rise of the dollar. With constant exchange rates, donations would have risen by 2.5 percent.
Merchandising and licencing, however, fell sharply to 1.3 million dollars from 10.2 million dollars in 1995 when Brent Spar and French nuclear campaigns helped raise public awareness of the group.
Greenpeace's number of supporters dipped by around 2,000, but it said it was not unduly worried by the fall as the number of long-term supporters, whose financial support was greater, was growing.
The organisation said about 2.9 million people had contributed to its funds in the 18 months to the start of 1997.
